prime.problem: Lecture 2 is two hours of small tensor steps that build the same model twice. Read card by card, it is easy to come away with a counting script and a training script and no map of how they connect: which parts define the model, which parts judge it, and why the slower route is the one the series keeps.
prime.fits: The front page of the bigram course. It builds on micrograd's update rule w ← w − lr · ∂L/∂w (lecture 1) and puts all ten bigram cards on one formula: a loss that judges P, and two ways to fill P.
expect: the average NLL as the one score (0 perfect, 3.2958 uniform)
route 1: count, add k, normalise each row
route 2: one-hot @ W, softmax, gradient descent
W ≈ log(N + 1) and L2 = fake counts
the two silent failures: keepdim and zero counts
prime.goal: Explain the whole lecture from the one formula: say which side each card works on, give the loss each route reaches (2.4540 counting, 2.4729 after 100 net steps), and name the three limits the next course removes.

attend: In the core formula, which cards work on the loss side and which on the P side, and where does the sampling card fit if it touches neither?
Each lever in the table moves one term of the formula. Which lever moves the counting route's P, and which lever does the same job in the neural route?
Why does the page call both the keepdim bug and a zero count "silent", and which number in the levers table gives each away?
The net starts at 3.7590, worse than the 3.2958 of blind guessing. What does the formula say it would start at with W = 0, and why?
Which three things does the closing note say this lecture leaves undone, and which card's number shows each one?

must: One loss judges every model: average −log P[x, y] over the 228,146 real bigrams → 0 would be perfect and 1/27 everywhere scores log 27 = 3.2958 → the row-normalised counts maximise the likelihood → no bigram model goes below 2.4540 on these names

Route 1: count pairs into N → add k to every cell → divide each row by its own total (keepdim) → P; k = 0 leaves 102 zero cells and an infinite loss on unseen pairs, k = 1 fixes it for 2.4540 → 2.4546

Route 2: one-hot(x) @ W is row W[x] → softmax exponentiates and normalises it, so W plays log counts → gradient descent on the same loss walks W toward log(N + 1) (3.7590 → 2.4729 in 100 steps, from above)

Pulling W toward 0 makes every row uniform → the L2 term 0.01 · mean(W²) does in route 2 what k does in route 1 → both trade training loss for sane probabilities on rare or unseen pairs, so their strength must be tuned on names the model hasn't seen
elevated: Counting needs a table row for every possible context (27ᵏ rows: 19,683 for 3 characters) → it can't grow → route 2 keeps the loss, backward and update and only changes how the logits are computed → the series keeps route 2 even though it is slower and no better here
Rare rows get gradient only from their own examples (q starts 272 of 228,146) → they converge slowest → after 100 regularised steps the net's P[qu] is 0.3548 where smoothed counts give 0.6923
reference: the card-by-card numbers: 32,033 names, 102 zero cells, 7.0225, 3.4834, 3.7693
the full k sweep (+10 2.4621 … +100000 3.2837) and the step-by-step losses
seed 2147483647 and the torch 2.14 samples, which differ from the video's

compress.prompt: Page closed: draw the course's causal map around the core formula. Put the loss in the middle with its scale (0, 2.4540, 3.2958, ∞). Above it, route 1 feeding P; below it, route 2 feeding P with the backward arrow into W. Mark the two silent failures in red, draw the two links between the routes, and write beside the whole thing the three limits that send you to the next lecture.
checklist: loss = −(1/n) Σ log P[xᵢ, yᵢ]; 0 perfect, 3.2958 uniform, 2.4540 the floor for a bigram on these names
route 1: N → + k → ÷ row sum with keepdim → P; without keepdim row 0 sums to 7.0225; with k = 0 a zero count gives ∞
route 2: xs → one-hot → @ W → exp → ÷ row sum → −log p[y] → mean → backward → W −= 50 · W.grad
the links: W ≈ log(N + 1) (2.4546 when set by hand), and L2 on W = fake counts
the limits: one character of context, a table that grows 27× per character, losses measured on training data

retrieve.q: Using only the core formula, explain why a model that learned nothing scores 3.2958 and why no bigram model can score below 2.4540 on the training names.
answer: learned nothing = P is 1/27 everywhere, so every term is −log(1/27) = log 27 = 3.2958
the loss is minimised by the P that maximises the likelihood of the training bigrams
for a bigram that P is exactly the row-normalised counts, which score 2.4540, so both routes can only reach it

retrieve.q: Follow the first bigram of 'emma', .e, through both routes to the number it adds to the loss. Name each object and its shape.
answer: route 1: row 0 of N (27 counts, summing to 32,033) → divide by 32,033 → P[0, 5] = 1,531 / 32,033 = 0.0478 → −log = 3.0408
route 2: x = 0 → one-hot row of 27 → @ W (27×27) gives the logits W[0] → exp and ÷ row sum → probs[0]
with the random W, probs[0, 5] = 0.0123 → −log = 4.3993; training moves it toward the counting value

retrieve.q: A teammate proposes dropping route 2 from the course: counting is exact, one pass and has no learning rate. What does the course lose, and when are they right?
answer: right for a true bigram: counting reaches 2.4540 exactly; the net only gets to 2.4729 in 100 steps and 2.4624 in 200
lost: the loop (forward, backward, update) that stays unchanged when the logits come from an MLP or a transformer
counting can't scale: 27ᵏ table rows for k characters of context, most of them empty

retrieve.q: Both fake counts and the L2 term raise the training loss. How would you choose their strength, and why is the training loss the wrong judge?
answer: on training names the loss always prefers none: k = 0 gives 2.4540, k = 1 gives 2.4546; the L2 net gives 2.4901 vs 2.4729
what they buy only shows on unseen names: 'andrejq' goes from ∞ to 3.4834
so tune the strength on a held-out dev split (Karpathy's E02 and E03)

compare.q: Micrograd's course comes down to one rule, w ← w − lr · ∂L/∂w. This course comes down to a loss and two ways to fill P. What does this course add around that rule, and which part does it take over unchanged?
answer: unchanged: the loop (forward, zero the gradients, backward, step), and W.grad = None is micrograd's zero_grad
added: a dataset of (x, y) pairs, a model whose output is a probability distribution, and the average NLL instead of squared error
added: a second route to the answer (counting) that tells you where gradient descent should land, 2.4540
different scale: 729 weights in one tensor and 228,146 examples per step, so lr 50 instead of micrograd's 0.1

compare.q: The big-ideas card splits the lecture into six claims; this page puts it on one formula. When is each view the better one to study from?
answer: the formula view: to place a new idea (which side, which lever) and to see that both routes minimise the same thing
the big-ideas view: to redraw each mechanism on its own and recall its number
use the formula first as a map, the six claims to fill it in, then the checkpoints to test both

predict.q: The next course gives the model 3 characters of context. Commit first: how many rows would a counting table need, and what would its loss on held-out names tell you that this course's 2.4540 can't?
predict.answer: 27³ = 19,683 rows of 27 cells each, most never seen, so counting is out and the MLP learns an embedding per character instead. A held-out (dev) loss shows whether the model generalises, which a training-set loss can't: the next course splits the names 80/10/10 and its final model reaches about 2.13 on train and 2.17 on dev (notebook values), well below the bigram's 2.45.

apply.task: Score both routes with the same line of code. Count N over all 228,146 bigrams, then compute the counting loss vectorised as -P[xs, ys].log().mean() for k = 0 and k = 1. Then treat log(N + 1) as if it were a trained W: pass its rows torch.log((N + 1).float())[xs] as logits to F.cross_entropy with ys. Try log(N) too.
apply.done: The vectorised counting loss prints 2.4540 (k = 0) and 2.4546 (k = 1); F.cross_entropy on log(N + 1) rows prints 2.4546 and on log(N) rows 2.4540 (computed on torch 2.14, under 1 s). That is the whole lecture in four numbers: counts as logits are the net's destination.
apply.hint: log(0) is −∞, but no real training bigram has a zero count, so the log(N) version still gives a finite loss.
